newsitem.title: UK: Lease rates climb as central bank fears hit gold.
newsitem.headline: Lease rates climb as central bank fears hit gold.

text.p: Gold lease rates climbed on Tuesday and Wednesday as the availability of metal to borrow tightened ahead of the year end, dealers and analysts said.
But they also offered other explanations for the rates jumping from around 1.80 percent for a month on Monday to over $2.10 percent on Tuesday and Wednesday.

One source noted that shortly after the Reuters' GOFO page (showing gold lending rates) updated at 1100 GMT on Tuesday, fresh offers took rates back to around 1.85. However they were back up again by the same time on Wednesday.
Hovering behind the increase were persistent rumours of a European central bank selling gold as part of its compliance with the proposed European Monetary Union (EMU).

"The EMU has crystalised a lot of thinking about gold. Whether or not EMU goes ahead, central bank thinking about gold will never be the same again," said bullion analyst Andy Smith at Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS).
"Lease rates go up not necessarily because of a central bank. It could be short selling, but probably not extraordinary producer selling because the contango is too low," Smith said.

But he added that there was a "natural association" between central bank gold sales and lease rates as the banks were the main lenders to the market and a bank making a sale would stop lending thus tightening liquidity and raising rates.
Late last November gold lease rates went into backwardation -- near term borrowing rates are higher than longer term rates -- for the first time when one-month rates climbed to over six percent.
This was at the height of a forward selling campaign by the producers and coincided with the beginning of the central banks beginning to review their gold positions ahead of year end.
"The rise this week shocked everybody. It could be a throwback to last year when the market was very tight," one forward dealer said.
"There has definitely been good producer selling thrown forward and taking gold out of the market. Further, it's the courting season with the central banks," he said.
The tightness came from both demand and supply of available gold. "A chunk has been borrowed and there is also a bit of short term illiquidity," the dealer said.
"Because of last year, the market is very nervous and volatile near term but lease rates are not ridiculously high like last year. They are still under 2.5 percent," he added.
Two other explanations for high rates were a Swiss bank speculating in gold which added volatility and the hedge funds were short of gold, the forward dealer said.
"This is a volatile period and it will not go on happening for the next six months. The market is also a bit twitchy over year end -- especially after last year," a dealer said.
A repeat of last year's backwardation was unlikely, market sources said.
"More lending came into the market late last year and a lot of new lenders have stayed in the market. But at year end the supply side is not as flexible as usual," said UBS's Smith.
"Some borrowers may be jumping before the central banks have their end of year review. The interbank market gets naturally tighter nearing year end," he said.
Recent comments by Portugese and Belgian central bankers on whether or not they plan to sell gold has kept the market on edge, sources said.

"It is best not to say anything about gold. There appears to be a debate going on but the market wants gold to be a sterile reserve," Smith said. "Obviously the debate is over selling. Nobody expects the central banks to buy," he said.

Analysts said the Belgian comments were largely ignored by the market even although a major seller -- Belgium has sold over 700 tonnes of gold in four batches since 1991 -- said it would not be selling again.
The continuing concern over central banks liquidising gold assets meant that "the damage has been done to sentiment without selling an ounce," Smith said.
